issues.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement cannot withdraw an admission when doing so would displace the opposing party’s case and cause irretrievable prejudice.
material_facts: In a partition suit, the defendants’ original written statement admitted that seven listed properties were joint family properties and that the plaintiff had a share in them.
After the plaintiff sought appointment of a receiver for the admitted properties, a defendant sought to amend the written statement to withdraw the admission as to five of those properties.
Allowing the amendment would remove the basis for the plaintiff’s claim to a share in those properties, despite the possibility of a preliminary decree on the admitted position.
issues.conclusion: The amendment seeking to withdraw the admission as to the five properties was not permissible, and the High Court’s order allowing that amendment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an amendment to a written statement cannot withdraw an admission in favour of the plaintiff if the withdrawal would displace the plaintiff’s case and cause irretrievable prejudice. Order XV Rule 1 supported the conclusion that, where the parties were not at issue on the admitted properties, the plaintiff could have sought judgment on that basis. Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. governs; Akshaya Restaurant v. P. Anjanappa was contrary to that binding three-judge decision to the extent that it permitted such a prejudicial withdrawal and was treated as per incuriam. Basavan Jaggu Dhobi v. Sukhnandan Ramdas Chaudhary was distinguishable because the alternative plea there did not displace an admission in the plaintiff’s favour.

rule.if: partition_suit and defense_admitted_claimant_share and amendment_withdraws_admission and withdrawal_would_displace_claim and withdrawal_would_irretrievably_prejudice_claimant

predicates.partition_suit: The claimant brought a civil action seeking division of jointly held property.
predicates.defense_admitted_claimant_share: The defending party’s written statement admitted that the claimant had a share in specified property.
predicates.amendment_withdraws_admission: The defending party sought to change its written statement to retract an earlier admission.
predicates.withdrawal_would_displace_claim: Retracting the admission would remove the basis of the claimant’s case concerning the property.
predicates.withdrawal_would_irretrievably_prejudice: The claimant would lose a benefit accrued from the admission, including the ability to obtain judgment on the admitted position.

issues.definition: When a defending party seeks to retract an admission in a partition suit and doing so would displace the claimant’s case and cause irretrievable prejudice, the amendment must be refused.

issues.legal_issue: A written statement may be amended to add an allegation about possession when the allegation does not withdraw an admission or prejudice the opposing party’s case.
material_facts: From the outset, the defendants denied that the plaintiff had an interest in the Schedule-B properties.
The proposed amendment added that those properties were in the possession of trespassers.
The amendment did not withdraw an admission in the plaintiff’s favour or otherwise displace the plaintiff’s case concerning those properties.
issues.conclusion: The amendment concerning the Schedule-B properties remained allowed; the Supreme Court declined to interfere with that part of the High Court’s order, while observing that the High Court should not have interfered under its revisional jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendment of a written statement may be permitted where it does not withdraw an admission in the plaintiff’s favour or cause prejudice by displacing the plaintiff’s case. Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. establishes the restriction on amendments that withdraw prejudicial admissions; the circumstances here did not attract that restriction. The Court observed that the High Court had, strictly speaking, exceeded the limits of revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but declined to interfere with this part of its order in exercise of Article 136 of the Constitution.

rule.if: civil_suit and original_defense_denied_claimant_interest and amendment_adds_possession_allegation and amendment_does_not_withdraw_admission and amendment_does_not_prejudice_claimant

predicates.civil_suit: A claimant brought a civil action against a defending party.
predicates.original_defense_denied_claimant_interes: The defending party’s original written statement denied that the claimant had an interest in the property.
predicates.amendment_adds_possession_allegation: The defending party sought to add an allegation that the property was in the possession of trespassers.
predicates.amendment_does_not_withdraw_admission: The proposed change did not retract an admission previously made in the claimant’s favour.
predicates.amendment_does_not_prejudice_claimant: The proposed change did not displace the claimant’s case or adversely affect a right arising from an admission.

issues.definition: Where a defending party originally denied the claimant’s interest and seeks to add a possession allegation without withdrawing an admission or prejudicing the claimant, the amendment may be allowed.
